sources.entry: Using XSTATE features in user space applications - Defines the arch_prctl permission Linux requires for AMX tile data and the trap a tile instruction takes until granted.

summary.title: Using XSTATE features in user space applications
summary.one_liner: Learn how Linux user-space programs request permission via arch_prctl to use dynamically enabled CPU state such as AMX TILE_DATA, and what happens if they don't.
keywords: how to enable amx in linux
takeaways: Features like AMX TILE_DATA are enabled in XCR0 but the first use traps, because large XSAVE buffers are not allocated by default.
Call arch_prctl(ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM, feature_nr) to request permission; check availability first with ARCH_GET_XCOMP_SUPP.
Permission is per process, inherited across fork, and cleared on exec.
Alternate signal stacks must be large enough for the bigger signal frame once permission is granted; otherwise ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM returns -ENOSUPP and sigaltstack returns -ENOMEM.
Without permission, using the feature sends SIGILL; VM guest permissions must be requested before the first VCPU is created.
summary.summary: This kernel documentation page explains how x86 user-space applications discover and request dynamically enabled XSTATE features, using AMX TILE_DATA as the main example. It describes the arch_prctl options (ARCH_GET_XCOMP_SUPP, ARCH_GET_XCOMP_PERM, ARCH_REQ_XCOMP_PERM), why signal alternate stacks must be sized for the larger XSAVE frame, and how the first trapped instruction is handled. A C code example shows checking AMX support and requesting tile data permission, and the page closes with signal frame behavior and guest VM permission variants.
